Package com.cognizant.emk.multiagent.infrastructure.ratelimit

Class Bucket4jRateLimitGate

java.lang.Object
com.cognizant.emk.multiagent.infrastructure.ratelimit.Bucket4jRateLimitGate
All Implemented Interfaces:
RateLimitConfigChangeListener, RateLimitGate
@Component public class Bucket4jRateLimitGate extends Object implements RateLimitGate, RateLimitConfigChangeListener
Single in-JVM Bucket4j bucket with two stacked bandwidths (per-minute and per-hour). REQ-RL-002 / REQ-RL-003 / REQ-RL-004 / REQ-RL-005.

Two stacked bandwidths in one Bucket: Bucket4j's tryConsumeAndReturnRemaining returns a ConsumptionProbe that aggregates over all bandwidths. When a request is denied, the probe's getNanosToWaitForRefill() reports the wait until the most-restrictive bandwidth refills — exactly what Retry-After should reflect.

Live rebuild. The current Bucket sits behind a volatile reference. onRateLimitConfigChanged(com.cognizant.emk.multiagent.domain.ratelimit.RateLimitConfig) swaps it atomically when an admin updates the configuration. The previously-consumed tokens are NOT preserved across rebuild — see DESIGN-CHOICES.md for the trade-off ("the new bucket starts full; in-flight clients get a one-shot grace allotment up to perMinute"). At the v1 sizing (REQ-NFR-005) this is harmless.

Cold start. The bucket is built eagerly on ApplicationReadyEvent so the first request never pays the construction cost. If the seed row is missing, application startup fails loudly via the repository's IllegalStateException — operators must see it.

Retry-After rounding. Bucket4j returns nanoseconds; we ceil to the nearest second and floor at 1 so the client never sees Retry-After: 0 on a denied request.
